findings.text: Init entry announces start then follows exactly one path. When a benchmark selector is active it initializes a tree for range allocation, runs the selected benchmark, destroys the tree and jumps to final accounting. Otherwise it executes a long ordered functional suite with each group bracketed by initialization and destruction, covering deficiency, null store, expansion, iteration, forking, state handling, ranges, sequences, bounds splits, navigation, gap handling, spanning, fuzzing and cyclic allocation. It then synchronizes, reports passed against run totals, and succeeds only when the totals match.
Exit hook does nothing and exists only to balance the init entry for unload.

Init entry creates two null terminated pointer arrays, fills all but the terminator with freshly allocated records carrying opposite signed values and a shared marker, concatenates the arrays, verifies marker integrity, zero total, expected length and preserved order, releases all storage, logs outcome and returns zero only on full success.
Exit hook is empty because all allocations from the init path are already released before return.

Init entry runs page, heap and virtual memory, slab cache, and persistent RCU suites in order, accumulates total and failure counts across them, logs either complete success or a failure summary, and returns zero only when failures remain zero.
Init entry emits a greeting message and reports success without establishing persistent state.
Exit hook emits a farewell message and releases nothing.
Record holds a signed payload plus an unsigned integrity marker. The marker detects corruption or misordering after concatenation while the payloads are chosen to cancel out when summed.
Key wrapper contains a single unsigned identifier used to request an aggregated object.
World state contains a root counter, a delta counter, a scratch buffer for the next root, an array of per key object handles sized by key count, and a parallel array of per key reference counts.
Root pairs a key wrapper with a fixed capacity character buffer holding its aggregated representation.
Delta holds an unsigned separation between key identifiers used to exercise sharing across neighboring keys.
INPUT_MAX denotes 128. EXPECT denotes twice INPUT_MAX minus two, which evaluates to 254 and accounts for two terminators.
MAGIC denotes 0xf00ff00f, used as the integrity marker for test records.
GARBAGE_INT denotes 0x09A7BA9E for word sized soiling. GARBAGE_BYTE denotes 0x9E for trailing bytes.
CTOR_BYTES denotes the size of an unsigned integer. CTOR_PATTERN denotes 0x41414141 written by the constructor at object start.
BULK_SIZE denotes 100, the capacity of the static bulk pointer array used for grouped slab allocations.
NUM_KEYS denotes 32. BUF_LEN denotes 128. MAX_KEY_ID_DIFF denotes 5.

Each functional group runs against a freshly initialized tree that is destroyed before the next group begins. Benchmark selection is exclusive and bypasses the functional suite. Final status depends solely on equality of run and passed counters.

Concatenation preserves input order with all entries from the first array followed by all from the second, excluding terminators. Output length equals sum of populated entries. Opposite payloads sum to zero and every marker remains intact.

Fresh page blocks, heap buffers and virtual buffers are expected to contain only zeroes. The suites soil each allocation, release it, reallocate the same size, and treat any non-zero byte in the second allocation as failure.

Slab objects requested with zeroing are expected fully zeroed. Objects from a constructor cache are expected to carry the constructor pattern at start with the remainder soiled except for the pattern bytes. Non-RCU non-constructor objects are expected zeroed unless zeroing was not requested, while RCU objects are allowed to retain prior contents. Constructor and zeroing are never requested together.

Repeated requests for the same key identifier return the identical object handle while incrementing a per key reference count. Release decrements the count and forwards the stored handle. Release with a zero count does nothing. A differing handle for an already tracked key is treated as error and immediately released.
Key index translation is identity for identifiers below the key capacity. Identifiers at or above capacity trigger a warning and fold to index zero.
Soiling writes the word pattern repeatedly from an optional skip offset and fills any trailing partial word with the byte pattern. A skip larger than the size triggers a warning.
A helper scans a buffer byte by byte and returns the count of non-zero bytes, used as the zeroing oracle across all suites.
Per suite reporting logs either a failure summary with failing and total counts or a full pass message naming the calling routine and total count.
Log formatting prefixes every message with the module name followed by a separator, applied uniformly across all test modules in this lane.

Slab coverage iterates object sizes doubling from eight across ten steps. For each size it exercises all combinations of constructor, RCU and zeroing flags except the forbidden constructor plus zeroing pair, plus an additional bulk allocation check.
Combined heap and virtual coverage iterates twenty powers of two starting at one, testing each size with both allocators.
Page coverage iterates every page order defined by the order count, running one allocate soil release reallocate check cycle per order.

An RCU cache object that is freed is expected to retain its prior contents when the same storage is reallocated, verified by comparing a saved copy after reuse within 1024 attempts. Failure to observe reuse within the bound is treated as pass.

Grouped slab allocations are expected to return fully zeroed objects on first use. Each group is checked for non-zero bytes, soiled, and released before the next iteration, repeating groups of ten for up to 1024 iterations or until a failure appears.

RCU read side protection surrounds the sequence that copies an RCU slab object, frees it, then inspects the freed storage and compares against the copy. The lock ensures the storage remains safe to touch after free within the critical section.
A barrier synchronizes callbacks before the final passed versus run accounting in the tree suite, ensuring all deferred work has completed before status is decided.

Tree test machine starts in announcement, branches to either single benchmark or ordered functional chain, then moves to synchronization, reporting and terminal success or invalid status based on counter equality.
Concatenation test machine moves from array allocation through population, concatenation, sequential validation of marker, total, length and order, to release and terminal pass or invalid status.

Slab object test machine cycles per iteration through allocation, validation, soiling and release, with an RCU variant that inserts copy, free under read protection, post-free validation and comparison before unlock. Ten cycles complete before cache destruction.

Aggregated object reference machine starts untracked, stores the handle on first acquisition, shares it on subsequent acquisitions with incremented count, decrements on release, and returns to untracked only after the count reaches zero.
Skip exceeding the buffer size triggers a warning before size adjustment. Callers must ensure the skip never exceeds the size to avoid underflow in the remaining length computation.

Out of range key identifiers collapse to index zero after a warning, so distinct invalid keys alias the same slot and reference count. Callers must keep identifiers within capacity to avoid silent aliasing.
Inspecting slab storage after free is safe only inside an RCU read side critical section for RCU caches. The same inspection outside protection or for non-RCU caches would be use after free.

Allocation failures at any stage lead to failure accounting and unwind of already acquired storage without dereference. Output validation bounds its scan to prevent overreading when concatenation is malformed.

Tree and memory suites signal failure by a single invalid return after logging, with no partial success distinction. Any mismatch between run and passed totals or any recorded failure yields the same error.
